title: Attribution Graph Coverage as a Function of Prompt Length: Where Does Tracing Break Down?

original_idea.problem: Anthropic reports ~25% prompt coverage for attribution graphs. The failure modes have not been systematically characterized.
original_idea.direction: Run the attribution graph pipeline on prompts stratified by token length and semantic type. Record coverage rate, graph density, and fraction of variance explained. Identify which prompt types cause failures.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: knowing the failure distribution is prerequisite to improving coverage. If failures concentrate in safety-relevant prompt types (instruction following, deception detection), that identifies an urgent gap in interpretability tools. Directly informs where to focus research for scalable oversight.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Running attribution graph tools requires familiarity with circuit-tracing methodology. Constructing stratified prompt sets requires understanding of semantic categories. Interpreting graph density and variance explained requires mechanistic interpretability background. Not beginner-accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-defined: run the pipeline on curated prompts, record metrics, plot coverage vs. prompt features. The deliverable (coverage-by-category heatmap) is clear. The main risk is tool setup time, but if tools work, the experiment is bounded.

novelty.reasoning: Anthropic's original circuit tracing papers (March 2025) acknowledge the ~25% coverage rate and note that the methods succeed on some prompts and fail on others, but do not systematically characterize failure modes by prompt length or semantic type. The open-source release (May 2025) enabled community experimentation, but no published work has systematically stratified prompts by token length and semantic category to map the coverage boundary. The Neuronpedia landscape survey and blog posts discuss limitations qualitatively but not quantitatively. This systematic characterization remains a genuine gap.
